title: The Maximum Voltage
question: In Milgram's baseline setup, about two-thirds of ordinary participants delivered the maximum 450-volt shock when the experimenter instructed them to continue.
correctExplanation: True. Roughly 65% went to 450V despite protests, sweating, and screams. Ordinary people, extraordinary compliance.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. The baseline number — 26 of 40 to maximum — shocked psychology itself. Protests accompanied obedience; almost nobody enjoyed it, yet most continued.
lessonContent:
Ordinary people comply extraordinarily under authority.
Protests accompany obedience more than prevent it.
Baselines anchor every variation after.
Two-thirds is the number that changed ethics.
Share this: quote 65% before judging anyone.

title: The Closer Victim
question: Moving the suffering learner into the same room as the teacher increased obedience, since closeness builds empathy that overrides orders.
correctExplanation: False. Proximity collapsed obedience (to ~40%, touch-proximity ~30%): closeness empowers refusal, not compliance. Distance enables harm.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. Same-room suffering cut obedience sharply; forced touch cut it further. Empathy needs proximity to activate — remote victims suffer most from compliance.
lessonContent:
Proximity empowers refusal reliably.
Distance enables harm more than closeness.
Empathy needs nearness to activate.
Remote suffering obeys smoothest.
Share this: close one distance deliberately.

title: The Phone Orders
question: When the experimenter issued orders by telephone instead of standing nearby, obedience rates stayed essentially identical to baseline.
correctExplanation: False. Absent authority collapsed compliance to ~20%: many participants improvised lower shocks or quit. Presence pressures; distance liberates.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. Telephone orders bled authority badly — a fifth obeyed versus two-thirds present. Voices without bodies command weakly; proximity is pressure.
lessonContent:
Presence pressures; absence liberates measurably.
Voices without bodies command weakly.
Authority attenuates across distance fast.
Nearness is pressure's delivery system.
Share this: hang up on one remote order.

title: The Divided Coats
question: When two experimenters visibly disagreed about continuing, obedience fell to nearly zero — every participant stopped and sided against cruelty.
correctExplanation: True. Divided authority paralyzes compliance: with no single legitimate voice, participants halted. Unity commands; disagreement frees.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. Two lab coats arguing collapsed the spell completely — zero full obedience. Legitimacy needs unanimity; visible dissent among authorities liberates subjects instantly.
lessonContent:
Divided authorities liberate subjects instantly.
Unanimity is legitimacy's load-bearing wall.
Visible dissent breaks spells completely.
Two coats arguing free every teacher.
Share this: voice one dissent that frees others.

title: The Rebelling Peers
question: Adding two confederate 'teachers' who refuse to continue had little effect — real participants kept obeying at baseline rates regardless.
correctExplanation: False. Peer rebellion crashed obedience to ~10%: seeing refusal modeled made refusing possible. One dissenter frees dozens silently waiting.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. Confederate refusers demolished compliance — modeling dissent matters more than feeling it. Permission structures, not private doubts, decide obedience.
lessonContent:
Modeled dissent matters more than felt doubt.
One refuser frees dozens silently waiting.
Permission structures decide obedience rates.
Peers outweigh experimenters in courage markets.
Share this: model one refusal publicly.

title: The Seedy Office
question: Moving the experiment from prestigious Yale to a run-down Bridgeport office made essentially no difference to obedience rates.
correctExplanation: False. Bridgeport obedience fell to ~48%: prestige legitimizes cruelty measurably. Lab coats need impressive buildings behind them.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. Yale's marble bought seventeen extra points of compliance over a shabby storefront. Legitimacy cues — architecture included — calibrate obedience precisely.
lessonContent:
Marble buys compliance measurably.
Prestige legitimizes cruelty point by point.
Settings calibrate obedience precisely.
Storefronts free what campuses bind.
Share this: discount one marble hallway.

title: The German Question
question: Follow-up studies across cultures found obedience effects broadly similar outside America — the pattern was never a German or American specialty.
correctExplanation: True. Replications from Munich to Amman to Australia return comparable rates: situations, not national characters, drive compliance. No culture holds a monopoly on obedience.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. The 'authoritarian culture' excuse died in replication: Jordanians, Germans, Australians obeyed alike. Situations export perfectly; dispositions explain little.
lessonContent:
Situations export; characters stay local.
Replication kills cultural excuses cleanly.
No nation monopolizes obedience or defiance.
Human is the relevant nationality here.
Share this: retire one national stereotype.

title: The Modern Cap
question: Jerry Burger's 2009 partial replication — stopping at 150 volts for ethics — found obedience patterns closely matching Milgram's era.
correctExplanation: True. Capped at the 150V decision point, modern participants refused at nearly identical rates to 1960s ones. Decades changed ethics rules, not human responses.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. Burger's ethical redesign preserved the crucial comparison: pre-150V behavior matched across half a century. Modernity flatters itself; the lab does not.
lessonContent:
Decades change rules, rarely responses.
Capped replications preserve crucial comparisons.
Modernity flatters itself without evidence.
150 volts still divides eras identically.
Share this: doubt one 'we've evolved' claim.

title: The Television Volt
question: A French TV show replicated Milgram as a game show, with an audience cheering — and obedience ran even higher, near 80%.
correctExplanation: True. 'Game of Death' showed cameras plus crowds outrank lab coats: 64 of 80 shocked to maximum. Entertainment legitimizes what science merely requests.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. Beauvois's televised version out-obeyed Yale: audiences and spotlights added authority no ethics board approved. Applause commands louder than clipboards.
lessonContent:
Applause commands louder than clipboards.
Cameras add authority ethics never approved.
Entertainment legitimizes beyond science.
Crowds amplify orders measurably.
Share this: distrust one cheering crowd.

title: The Agent Excuse
question: Milgram argued participants entered an 'agentic state' — seeing themselves as instruments of authority, responsibility shifted upward.
correctExplanation: True. The agentic shift explains the catchphrase 'just following orders': self as instrument, authority as author. Responsibility outsourced feels like responsibility absent.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. Subjects repeatedly said the experimenter was responsible — agency transferred, conscience muted. Instruments don't deliberate; that was precisely the state induced.
lessonContent:
Instruments don't deliberate by definition.
Responsibility outsourced feels absent entirely.
Agentic shifts mute private conscience.
Authorship assigned upward absolves downward.
Share this: reclaim one outsourced agency.

title: The Shifted Blame
question: When debriefed, obedient participants typically claimed full personal responsibility and rejected any suggestion the experimenter shared blame.
correctExplanation: False. Participants overwhelmingly assigned responsibility to the experimenter ('he told me to'): blame flowed upward, never inward.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. Debriefings record blame flowing upward: subjects insisted the experimenter owned the consequences. Responsibility shifted exactly as the agentic theory predicts — outward, upward, away.
lessonContent:
Blame flows upward under authority reliably.
'I was told to' is the agentic motto.
Outward, upward, away: blame's escape route.
Ownership evaporates inside hierarchies.
Share this: own one ordered act fully.

title: The Universal Obedience
question: Milgram's headline finding was that essentially all participants obeyed to the maximum — disobedience was vanishingly rare.
correctExplanation: False. Thirty-five percent refused outright — heroes exist in every condition. Headlines remember the obedient; data honors the refusers too.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. Fourteen of forty defied the experimenter completely at baseline. Obedience dominated but never monopolized: minorities refuse in all conditions.
lessonContent:
Minorities refuse in all conditions studied.
Headlines remember sheep; data keeps goats.
Thirty-five percent is a large resistance.
Honor refusers alongside the obedient.
Share this: join one baseline minority.

title: The Scream Stopper
question: The learner's agonized screams and demands to be freed ended the session for most participants, who stopped shocking immediately.
correctExplanation: False. Screams accompanied continued shocking for the majority — protests without exit. Agony registered; compliance continued anyway.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. The 300-volt wall of protest stopped almost nobody: two-thirds marched past screams to 450V. Hearing suffering differs entirely from heeding it.
lessonContent:
Hearing differs entirely from heeding.
Screams accompany compliance routinely.
Protest without exit changes nothing.
Agony registered still gets overridden.
Share this: heed one scream fully.

title: The Gender Gap
question: Milgram found women obeyed at dramatically lower rates than men, suggesting conscience tracks gender strongly.
correctExplanation: False. An all-female run matched male rates (~65%): conscience shows no gender gap under authority. Stereotypes of gentler refusal died in the data.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. Women obeyed identically (though with more visible distress): situation swamps gender completely. Gentler-sex theories found no support in the voltage logs.
lessonContent:
Situations swamp gender completely here.
Distress differs; compliance matches exactly.
Stereotypes die in voltage logs.
Conscience shows no gender gap found.
Share this: retire one gendered virtue claim.

title: The Born Follower
question: Authoritarian personality scores strongly predicted who obeyed — dispositions, not situations, drove Milgram's results.
correctExplanation: False. Personality predicted weakly; condition variations predicted massively. Milgram's thesis is situational: contexts, not characters, explain compliance.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. F-scale scores barely moved the needle while room layouts swung obedience forty points. Dispositions decorate; situations decide — the field's founding lesson.
lessonContent:
Contexts decide where characters decorate.
Room layouts swing forty points easily.
Personality barely moves obedience needles.
Situations explain; dispositions describe.
Share this: blame one room, not one soul.

title: The Willing Sadist
question: Milgram's volunteers were disproportionately sadistic — they enjoyed delivering pain, which explains the high obedience rates.
correctExplanation: False. Participants sweated, trembled, protested, and begged to stop — enjoyment was vanishingly rare. Obedience tortured the obedient too.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. Observers record anguish, not pleasure: nervous laughter, seizures of tension, desperate glances. Compliance without joy is precisely what makes the finding terrifying.
lessonContent:
Anguish accompanied obedience routinely.
Enjoyment was vanishingly rare throughout.
Compliance tortures the compliant too.
Joyless obedience terrifies most of all.
Share this: pity one obedient sufferer.

title: The Grateful Subject
question: In follow-up surveys, the large majority of Milgram's participants said they were glad to have taken part, with almost none regretting it.
correctExplanation: True. Roughly 84% reported gladness versus ~1% regret: subjects valued the self-knowledge purchased with distress. Ethics debates rage; participants mostly endorsed.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. Follow-ups show overwhelming endorsement: painful afternoons bought lasting insight most prized. Debriefings plus time converted trauma into education, by subjects' own accounts.
lessonContent:
Distress purchased insight most prized.
Endorsement followed debriefing plus time.
Subjects judge ethics by their own lights.
Painful afternoons educated willingly.
Share this: ask what distress taught you.

title: The Consent Legacy
question: Outrage over Milgram's deception helped drive modern informed-consent rules and ethics boards governing human research.
correctExplanation: True. Deception without full consent became the cautionary tale behind IRBs and consent codes. One lab's methods rewrote every lab's permissions.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. Baumrind's critiques plus public shock converted Milgram into regulation: review boards now gatekeep human studies worldwide. Controversy institutionalized into procedure.
lessonContent:
Controversy institutionalizes into procedure.
Cautionary tales rewrite permissions globally.
Deception debates built modern gates.
One lab reformed ten thousand.
Share this: thank one ethics board.

title: The Ordinary Finding
question: Milgram's core conclusion was that horrific obedience requires disturbed or evil personalities — monsters, not neighbors.
correctExplanation: False. The conclusion inverts it: ordinary neighbors suffice — situations manufacture compliance from the unremarkable. Monstrousness is optional equipment.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. 'Just ordinary people' is the terrifying thesis: no pathology required, no sadism needed. Neighbors suffice wherever authority structures the scene.
lessonContent:
Neighbors suffice where monsters were assumed.
Unremarkable people comply remarkably.
Pathology is optional equipment here.
Ordinary is the terrifying finding.
Share this: suspect one ordinary neighbor (lovingly).

title: The Nearby Coat
question: Obedience held steady whether the experimenter stood beside the teacher or issued orders from another room entirely.
correctExplanation: False. Nearby authority compels; distant authority merely suggests (65% versus ~20%). Steadiness across distance is precisely what the data refutes.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. Same-room orders versus telephone orders differ massively (~65% vs ~20%): nearness is pressure. This statement claims steadiness across distance, which the data refutes.
lessonContent:
Nearness is pressure, measurably.
Distance liberates measurably too.
Steadiness claims fail against gradients.
Coats nearby compel; phones suggest.
Share this: measure one authority gradient.

title: The White Coat
question: Symbols of legitimate expertise — lab coats, clipboards, prestigious addresses — measurably raise compliance with instructions.
correctExplanation: True. Legitimacy cues calibrate obedience: coats, titles, and marble each buy compliance points. Authority dresses for the effect it wants.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. Yale versus storefront, uniform versus casual: trappings move needles reliably. Costumes command because minds outsource vetting to symbols.
lessonContent:
Costumes command reliably worldwide.
Symbols outsource vetting efficiently.
Marble, coats, titles: compliance wardrobe.
Dress cues calibrate obedience points.
Share this: undress one authority symbol.

title: The Small Steps
question: The 15-volt increments — tiny escalations from trivial to terrible — helped participants advance without ever deciding to do great harm.
correctExplanation: True. Gradual escalation dissolves decision points: each step is only slightly worse than the last accepted one. No single shock feels like the moral cliff.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. Foot-in-the-door electrified: 15 volts more is always agreeable until 450. Great harms arrive in small, each-time-reasonable increments.
lessonContent:
Great harms arrive incrementally always.
Decision points dissolve under gradients.
Slightly-worse compounds into terrible.
Watch each step, not just cliffs.
Share this: notice one gradient today.

title: The Many Rooms
question: Milgram ran only one single experimental setup, so his findings rest on a single unrepeated observation.
correctExplanation: False. Milgram ran twenty-plus variations — proximity, prestige, peers, settings — mapping obedience's gradients systematically. Single setups never supported the thesis.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. The book reports a program, not an experiment: dozens of conditions isolate each variable. Replication lives inside the original work itself.
lessonContent:
Programs persuade where experiments suggest.
Dozens of conditions map gradients fully.
Variation is replication's first home.
Single setups never carried this thesis.
Share this: vary one condition deliberately.

title: The Nightingale Orders
question: In Hofling's hospital study, almost all nurses prepared to obey an unknown doctor's dangerous phone order — 21 of 22 began compliance.
correctExplanation: True. White coats by telephone commanded 95% initial compliance despite rule violations. Hospitals run on hierarchy deeper than protocol.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. Unknown voice, broken rules, lethal dose — yet white-coat authority overrode training in nearly every nurse. Hierarchy outranks protocol wherever coats speak.
lessonContent:
Hierarchy outranks protocol routinely.
Unknown voices command through coats.
Training yields to titles under pressure.
White coats override rulebooks daily.
Share this: question one hierarchy today.

title: The Assigned Cruelty
question: In Zimbardo's Stanford prison study, randomly assigned guards developed abusive behaviors within days, shaped by roles and setting.
correctExplanation: True. Random assignment plus uniforms plus basement produced cruelty in under a week — stopped early for ethics. Roles recruit behaviors fast.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. Coin flips made guards and prisoners; days made abusers and breakdowns. Situations cast faster than characters audition — the study's bleak casting call.
lessonContent:
Roles recruit behaviors within days.
Coin flips cast crueler than auditions.
Basements plus uniforms produce guards.
Situations direct; characters improvise.
Share this: notice one role recruiting you.
